To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cigarette smoking and dietary heterocyclic aromatic amine exposure are associated with microsatellite instability(+) colon cancer.

(1) cigarette smoking and dietary exposure to HAA are both associated with MSI(+) colorectal cancer, and that (2) the risk of MSI(+)-colon cancer associated with smoking remained significant after adjusting for high dietary exposure to HCA.
cigarette smoking and high dietary HAA exposures are associated with a specific subset (MSI(+) tumors) of colon cancers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the role of HAA in colon cancer etiology and the role of HCA in colon cancer progression.

the identification of dietary and lifestyle exposures that influence the development of MSI+ colon cancers, and the results of this study suggest that cigarette smoking and dietary heterocyclic aromatic amine exposure may play a role in colon carcinogenesis.
a subset of colon cancers with a unique molecular phenotype (MSI(+)) that is associated with a unique set of risk factors (cigarette smoking and high dietary HAA).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cigarette smoking and high dietary exposure to HAAs are both associated with a subset of colon cancers that are characterized by the microsatellite instability molecular pathway.
cigarette smoking and HAA exposure are associated with an increased risk of colon cancers with MSI(+) tumors.

the risk of MSI( + ) colon cancers increases with increasing dose (cigarette pack-years) and duration (years of cigarette smoking) of cigarette smoking, and with increasing dietary HAA exposure (high frequency of well-done meat eating, frying/barbecuing/broiling and use of meat drippings), independent of each other.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the risk of MSI( + ) colon cancer is significantly increased by both cigarette smoking and high dietary HAA, and that the risk of these exposures is additive.
cigarette smoking and high dietary exposure to HAA are associated with an increased risk of colon cancer with microsatellite instability.
the results of this study support the hypothesis that HAA exposure is an environmental risk factor for MSI(+) colon carcinogenesis.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the risk of developing MSI(+) colorectal cancer increases with increasing exposure to heterocycylic aromatic amines, which are found in cooked meat and are formed when the meat is charred, and with increasing exposure to cigarette smoking.
there are two important factors to consider in the prevention of colon cancer: smoking and diet.
there are specific subsets of colon cancers that have a strong association with smoking, red meat and HAA exposure.
